local_offer: We offer new starter visits to families these visits are to help your child to become familiar with the pre-school’s environment whilst still allowing for their initial need to have a close and familiar adult on hand to offer support. These sessions also enable support such as individual care routines for children still in nappies or ongoing health/dietary requirements to be discussed before children commence at pre-school. We are able to administer prescribed medicines once the appropriate form has been completed. If additional training is required to administer medicine, we will undertake this as necessary. We have a range of policies and procedures in place that ensure your child’s wellbeing. Copies of all policies are available in the setting and individual copies can be requested from the manager. We pride ourselves on being an inclusive provision ensuring that children with behavioural difficulties are supported and included in the setting using positive behaviour management and strategies. Practitioners provide good role models for positive behaviour and receive regular and team training to ensure a consistent approach is given to all children. Should your child display unwanted behaviour we will always share our concerns with parents to promote a consistent approach between home and the setting. Activities will be adapted to ensure your child is able to interact fully with their environment, and visual strategies-such as a visual timetable/Makaton can be used to help them understand our routines. We are also able to undertake personal care such as nappy changing. The safety of your child is paramount. You are requested to sign your child in and out and are required to provide details of adults who are authorized to collect your child. We will not allow any child to leave the premises if the person collecting them has not been previously authorized to do so by the parent. We undertake daily area safety/suitability checks and risk assessments as deemed necessary on our equipment, environment, or activity. Additionally, risk assessments are completed before any trip including short walks around the local community.  What outcomes does your setting, service or activity aim to achieve for children and young people with SEND and their families? Our staff team are highly qualified with the majority holding a level 3 in early years education. We work with all professionals as required for each child and always encourage these persons to come and visit the relevant children in the setting. If required, we will contact and work with the Buckinghamshire Council “Early Years’ Service”. We will obtain parental consent before contact is made and we will include parents in all decisions made and meetings held. If speech and language concerns are identified by the setting, we will advise the parents to take their child to the Speech and Language. We will advise the parents to contact the telephone advice line 01296 566045. We will also advise parents to look at some relevant websites i.e. https://www.bbc.co.uk/tiny-happy-people and https://hungrylittleminds.campaign.gov.uk/ Initially we arrange for you and your child to visit the setting to meet with the manager and staff. On acceptance of the place your child will be allocated a key person. The role of the key person is to build up a trusting relationship with both you and your child. They will establish a starting point in your child’s development by gathering information from you and by carrying out setting observations. Linking these observations to the early year’s development matters will help us to identify any concerns that we may have with your child’ s progress. We would discuss these concerns with you as soon as possible and with your consent would liaise with other professionals for support. A second visit will be arranged where you and your child will meet with the key carer to complete an "All about me" document. A 2-year-old check will be completed by key carer and parents on any 2-year-old who attends the setting, this may highlight any areas of concern. What recent SEND-specific training has been completed by your staff and/or volunteers? The setting SENCo has attended the initial and advanced SENCo training, recently achieved a level 3 qualification for an advanced SENCO (April 2024). We have also have a second trained SENCO, she completed the Initial SENCO training in October 2025, and she has just started her Level 3 Advanced training, due to complete in June 2026. Our Early Years Manager is responsible for ensuring our staff team has training in all relevant areas. The manager maintains individual training plans and provides training sessions when required. All staff receive training in behaviour management, speech and language and assessing children’s development. The SENCO attends termly Early Years SENCO Liaison Group meetings to remain up to date with current policies and procedures. We continually reflect upon our practice and will attend/offer training when a particular need is identified for example, Makaton. Staff training records are held on file and relevant training can be viewed on request. How do you involve parents and how can I get involved? We have an open-door policy and promote and value all parents’ views and opinions, having a strong relationship between the setting and parents is important to the preschool. We encourage ongoing dialogue with their child’s key worker, and you are welcome to speak to us at any time about your child’s development, however we encourage parents to email or phone us directly if they have any comments or concerns. Our highly qualified staff team ensures your child’s needs are quickly identified and supported, this in turn will be shared with you. Where your child has an individual support plan you will also be invited to review this regularly with your child key person and SENCO. Suggestions for ways to support learning in the home will also be discussed. Parents are invited to help in the setting and are encouraged to share their interests and skills. Your child will have a home preschool diary which is written in weekly, we also value your contribution of news from home in these books too (this needs to be removed). A weekly email will be sent to parents, telling them about the activities the children have been involved with during the week. We produce a newsletter half- termly. Termly parent’s meetings are scheduled with your child’s key person to discuss progress. How will you share information with me about my child’s progress? What is additional for children with SEND? The Manager and Special Educational Needs Co-ordinator (SENCO) will work closely with you and other professionals to determine your child’s needs. We have regular team meetings so that all practitioners have an understanding of your child’s needs. In addition, the Key Person will be able to identify any additional support through the observation procedure required by the Early Years Foundation Stage and individual plans will be made as necessary. We would involve the Buckinghamshire Council and Early Years’ Service, with your permission, asking them to advise us of any additional support they consider necessary. All children’s individual needs are closely monitored and where additional equipment is required this is purchased if feasible. Where necessary we can apply for additional funding from Buckinghamshire Council “Local Authority” to provide specialist equipment or additional adult support for individual children. How accessible is the environment (indoors and outdoors)? We will work closely with all parents to access any specialist equipment that may be required. There is a small step at the front entrance of the building which can be adapted for ramp use if necessary. There is also one step to the garden from the back preschool entrance however we can access the garden from the front door entrance, once outside there is an adequate area of level ground. We use Visual timetables to assist children with the daily routine. How can children and young people with SEND and their families start to use your service or activity? When your child joins, we offer a flexible settling in policy. They are initially invited to visit the setting to familiarise themselves with the environment and their key worker. When your child starts with us, their needs are monitored daily with you being regularly informed via text or phone calls to ensure you are involved in any decisions made until your child has settled. We have close links with the local schools to ensure smooth transitions, this includes visits by the local teachers to our setting, followed by us accompanying the children on visits to their new schools. Group and individual transition meetings are arranged as required. The schools provide us with books showing photos of the classroom to facilitate discussions and offer visual reassurance. With your consent all of your child’s records of development, individual support plans and professional reports will be passed to a new setting/school. Your child’s key person will be responsible for monitoring your child’s progress. Where your child is identified as benefiting from additional support we will devise a SEN plan, to be reviewed regularly with yourself. We provide a higher adult: child ratio than statutory requirements which allows for a high level of adult support through 1:1 or small group work as required. We have a Special Educational Needs Coordinator (SENCo) who attends regular training, provides support to staff and monitors children individually and within small groups. Through ongoing assessment, key persons plan the next steps for their individual children, based on their individual interest and needs, ensuring that they can access all areas of the curriculum. Additional support may be sought from other professionals with your consent, as appropriate. Where additional support or resources are required, strategies will be implemented via an individual plan. What future plans do you have for developing your SEND provision? We will continue our work with Buckinghamshire Council however if the need was to arise, we would be happy to work with any other authorities or health providers ensuring that we support the child/ren, their families to fulfil any requirements needed. Our Pre-school will continue to offer a provision based on individual needs and we would endeavor to adapt/develop our provision as necessary in response to the individual needs of the child/children in our care.

name: Bearbrook Combined School, Pre-school
description: Bearbrook Pre-school is an inclusive setting within Bearbrook Combined School for children aged 2 to 4 years. We offer the Early Years Foundation Stage curriculum which is play-based learning. Our holistic approach enables us to work closely with not only our children but also our families to offer children the best start to their education.
organisation: Bearbrook Combined School and Pre-school Headteacher's Welcome Being a father of two children, I passionately believe that every child should experience an excellent education as it forms a firm, concrete base upon which a child’s life can be built. I am very proud to be a part of the school, as I am sure you will be. As a school, we are constantly striving to improve and at the heart of everything we do is the belief that we want every child and member of staff to be nurtured, inspired and ultimately achieve the very best they can. We work hard to ensure that Bearbrook Combined School and Pre-school is a vibrant, exciting learning community, where children enjoy their education and make accelerated progress in a stimulating environment. We are committed to developing the whole child through their creativity and diversity. Our aim is for children to grow into confident, happy, independent, lifelong learners who can function as successful members of the community. In order to achieve this, we have high expectations with regard to attitudes to learning and behaviour, so that the children are ready for learning, are respectful and as a result, can keep themselves and others safe. One of the essential ingredients is a very close partnership between home and school. With your help and co-operation, we can create opportunities for your child to make the best possible progress, thus ensuring that your child’s years at Bearbrook are happy and rewarding. Not only do we want to build close partnerships with our families but also with other local schools. As a result, we are very proud to have become an academy and joined the Great Learners Trust. The Great Learners Trust operates with a strong vision of providing all children with outstanding learning opportunities and ensuring the best education for all children regardless of their starting points, level of disadvantage or family background. They believe that every child can be a great learner and have a strong set of values that are very similar to those at Bearbrook. They will not dictate how we work or organise ourselves, but they will provide high-quality support and recognise our strengths. They value their staff and will be mindful of work-life balance. They are also local, which is an advantage. At Bearbrook, we operate an ‘open door’ system. Should you have a query concerning your child’s welfare, you are always more than welcome to come into school to discuss it with me or any of the staff, often without an appointment. In addition, Senior Leaders and I are at the gate regularly, either at the start or the end of a day. Parents are always welcome in the school and offers of help, either generally, or with a particular skill, are always gratefully received. Therefore, on behalf of myself, the staff and governors, I would like to welcome you and your child to Bearbrook Combined School and Pre-school. Marcus Faulkner Headteacher office@bcsglt.co.uk https://www.bearbrookschool.co.uk/

description: Claydon Courtyard is open daily and attracts visitors who want to enjoy good food, wish to enroll in a variety of courses and workshops, book a spa day, or buy something unique and beautiful. The Phoenix Kitchen serves local, fresh and seasonal food throughout the year. Choose from a selection of homemade cakes, brunches, lunches, afternoon teas, Sunday roasts, or simply enjoy a cup of our locally roasted Fairtrade coffee. With delicious daily specials and a children’s menu, there’s something for all the family. If you’re visiting with young children, we have plenty of open space at Claydon Courtyard, and the Phoenix Kitchen offers a children’s menu, a baby food warming facility, high chairs, and a toddler playpen. There’s also Florence Nightingale’s carriage and a lovely old fire engine to discover. Finally, do keep an eye on our events calendar and pick out something to come along to.

local_offer: I aim to provide the best home learning and nurturing environment for any child. I aim to give the families opportunities to access care for their children whatever their needs. Learning through play is key to my setting: the age and stage of the child is considered as well as their individual needs to ensure they enjoy their time with me.  What outcomes does your setting, service or activity aim to achieve for children and young people with SEND and their families? I aim to provide a caring environment where all children are welcomed and supported. I will make my best endeavours to meet the needs of all children so that they can take part in all aspects of my setting and reach their full potential. I will work closely with any involved professionals to help me to support the children. I will involve parents at every opportunity and work to support them as well as the children. What recent SEND-specific training has been completed by your staff and/or volunteers?  How do you involve parents and how can I get involved? I work in partnership with parents, priding myself on sharing information about their child’s learning, development, and progress on a regular basis in a manner which suits them. I ask parents to share information about their child’s likes and dislikes, the activities which they find difficult and those which they enjoy the most. I aim to ensure that activities are extended to support children to meet their potential within the setting and share ideas with parents for use at home. How will you share information with me about my child’s progress? What is additional for children with SEND? I observe and assess all children and where there is a particular need, I support the preparation and implementation of a joint action plan for the child. With parents’ permission I may involve other services. I provide increased opportunities for communication for families of children with SEND and are flexible in how I communicate, for example, in person, on phone, email or electronic messages. How accessible is the environment (indoors and outdoors)? My home is accessible to most children and families. I am on a regular bus route for those needing public transport, and although there is a small threshold to the front door it has been used for wheelchair access. I aim to find somewhere suitable for the children to rest when needed and would always discuss options with parents. My outdoor area is mainly laid to lawn with mature borders and shady trees, although not large it is accessible for most children; there is a small ramp from the kitchen door for ease of access for all children. How can children and young people with SEND and their families start to use your service or activity? All families are welcome to visit and meet me and see my home before making an application to attend. I have a welcome pack that includes most information parents need to know, but I am happy to answer any questions. When children arrive, I encourage families to complete an ‘All about Me’ sheet, provide family photos and any special comforters (regardless of age of the child). I encourage parents to have some ‘settling in visits’ with their child. As a childminder, I have links with several local schools and pre-schools. I am happy for practitioners from other settings to visit me before a child starts to help them to settle (whether new to me or moving on elsewhere). What future plans do you have for developing your SEND provision? I am constantly aware of the need for flexibility within my setting to ensure that children’s needs can be met. I access training as necessary. I will keep updated with new guidance from the Local Authority and use their website regularly. I am keen to develop any new strategies such as ‘Hungry Little Minds’ and would like to earn ‘Millie’s Mark’

name: Clean Slate: Support for Victims of Abuse
description: Mission: the purpose of Clean Slate is to provide support to adult victims of sexual, physical and emotional abuse in Oxfordshire. We aim to empower these people with skills that help them cope with daily life while dealing with the emotional struggles of their past. Approach: at Clean Slate we aim to provide an integrated approach, dealing with emotional support as well as teaching practical skills to cope with day-to-day life. We are currently the only service in Oxfordshire that provides long-term counselling to these people. As a result of this we have built up working relationships with local professionals. We are now accepting referrals from doctors, mental health teams, the police, social services as well as self-referrals. Each client has an initial assessment. A personal pathway is drawn up, which sets achievable goals and this is then continually assessed throughout the process. One to one counselling is provided along side enrolment on certain programmes depending on the specific needs of our client. These programmes often deal with very specific problems but will broadly fit into four categories: Improving health and wellbeing. Improving integration into society. Increasing personal safety and perception of safety. Improving experience of the criminal justice system.

Any concerns we may have will be discussed with their parents and we are happy to work with any professionals to enhance the childs learning and development should it be required.  What outcomes does your setting, service or activity aim to achieve for children and young people with SEND and their families? They can also answer questions and offer advice on other appropriate services. Professionals are very welcome to meet the child in our setting if that is desired. What recent SEND-specific training has been completed by your staff and/or volunteers? name: Cliveden, National Trust
description: Set high above the River Thames, Cliveden’s magnificent gardens and breath-taking views have been admired for centuries. Visit Cliveden and you’ll discover a series of gardens with impressive floral displays, distinctive topiary, and an outstanding sculpture collection as well as acres of woodlands to explore. There are lots of events and activities planned throughout the year including the school holidays to suit all ages and tastes. Upcoming programming includes: - ‘We’re Going on a Bear Hunt’ trail, suitable for pre-school ages and is running from 9 May to 5 July 2026. - Summer of Play will also be returning from 18 July to 6 September 2026. Both trails are free, pay admission on arrival or scan you National Trust membership card. Car parking is included in the admission price. Especially for families, there is a storybook themed play area, giant maze, and woodland play trail, and the gift shop, which was designed with families in mind. At Cliveden, there is a range of food outlets available on your visit. Whether your looking for a sit-down lunch or a coffee to go, there’s something to suit your needs. Head to the National Trust Cliveden website to find out more. Discover more about Cliveden’s long association with boating on the River Thames, including its connections to The Wind in the Willows and how you can hire a boat to experience this timeless pastime for yourself. ‘Boating at Cliveden’ operates daily from April to October, subject to river and weather conditions. Head to the ‘Boating at Cliveden’ website to book your family boat trip. From March to October step beyond the ordinary into a world once walked by royalty, visionaries, and the great minds who shaped history, on one of our guided House visits. House visits run every Monday, Tuesday and Thursday starting every 10 minutes from 11am to 12:30pm and last 30-minutes. Tickets available (on a first come, first served basis) from the Information Centre. Cliveden House is currently leased as a luxury country hotel and generally not open to National Trust Visitors.
organisation: Cliveden (Maidenhead) | National Trust Set high above the Thames with far-reaching views, Cliveden’s impressive gardens and majestic woodlands capture the grandeur of a bygone age. Follow in the footsteps of dukes, earls and royalty as you explore a series of gardens, each with their own special charm. From the formality of the Parterre with its vibrant floral displays to the quirky statuary and topiary in the Long Garden, the gardens will delight you in every season. For younger visitors, the Storybook Play Den encourages imaginations to run wild as you play amongst wooden carvings of favourite storybook characters whilst the 500 metres of winding paths in the Cliveden Maze make it a challenge for all ages to find the centre. The formal gardens give way to secluded glades, tree-lined avenues and picturesque riverside with miles of woodland walks to discover. The house is now a luxury hotel but you can take a peek inside by joining a short guided tour on Thursday or Sunday afternoons from April to end of August (timed ticket required). cliveden@nationaltrust.org.uk https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/cliveden

description: Bucks Youth Dance Company is a high-energy performance company for passionate young dancers aged 12 to 18 in Buckinghamshire. Our exceptional training programme develops technical, creative, and performance skills through contemporary practices, original choreography, and professional-level rehearsals every week. This year, we’re proud to have been selected for Making Moves with Sadler’s Wells, giving our dancers the opportunity to perform on a national platform. Our programme also embeds Rambert Grades, offering an internationally recognised framework to support each dancer’s growth and achievement. Beyond performance, dancers gain a 360° understanding of the dance world, from creating work and performing, to exploring participatory practice, technical production, and design. We work collaboratively, encouraging dancers to engage fully in the creative process both in and beyond the studio. Across the year, dancers perform at major events such as U.Dance, Honeycomb Festival, and Buckinghamshire New University’s Dance Show. We open pathways into further and higher education, conservatoire training, and careers in the arts, with optional Arts Award, placements, guest artist sessions, and theatre trips. Developed in association with Buckinghamshire New University, BYDC is co-led by Pippa Fisher-Coldwell and Louise Kelsey. We are proud partners of Young Creative Bucks and Pips Dance Academy.

local_offer: In line with the British and Irish Orthoptic Society (BIOS) description, the purpose of the service is to identify and correct visual difficulties that will in some way contribute to a child having a reading or specific learning difficulty. The clinic offers an Orthoptic assessment to assess if the eyes work well together (Binocular Vision) and look at the focusing mechanism (Accommodative ability) of the eyes. Depending on the outcome of this, a follow-up appointment will be offered in the VPD clinic to assess if the child has visual stress/discomfort and/or visual perception difficulties. It is recommended that the child be seen by a local Optometrist before they attend their Orthoptic assessment. The Orthoptist will: - Determine visual problems relating to reading and writing skills - Manage the visual processing difficulties in a child or young person-centred way - Offer support to parents and teachers - Offer advice and guidance to schools, colleges, and universities.  What outcomes does your setting, service or activity aim to achieve for children and young people with SEND and their families? Relief of symptoms of visual stress. Symptoms of visual stress may include blurring or moving print, problems copying from the board, letter, number reversal, missing words, lines when reading. What recent SEND-specific training has been completed by your staff and/or volunteers?  How do you involve parents and how can I get involved?  How will you share information with me about my child’s progress? What is additional for children with SEND?  How accessible is the environment (indoors and outdoors)?  How can children and young people with SEND and their families start to use your service or activity? How do I get to see a VPD specialist Orthoptist? Referrals to this service must be completed by a General Practitioner (GP), Optometrist, or Occupational Therapist (OT). Because of the nature of the testing and the visual difficulties that we are looking for, we do not normally accept referrals for children below the age of 7. This is because most of these visual difficulties are normal for younger children to experience (for example, losing their place when reading). If there is any concern that a child has any of these difficulties before the age of 7, we would suggest that they be taken to an Optometrist (Optician) for a glasses test in the first instance. What future plans do you have for developing your SEND provision?

name: Survivors of Bereavement by Suicide
description: We are the only organisation offering peer-to-peer support to all those over the age of 18 impacted by suicide loss in the UK. We help those bereaved by suicide to support each other at the time of their loss and in the months and years that follow. We are a self-help organisation that provides a safe, confidential environment in which bereaved people can share their experiences and feelings, giving and gaining support from each other. We also strive to improve public awareness and maintain contact with many other statutory and voluntary organisations. We offer peer-led support groups, online virtual support groups, national telephone support lines, online community forums and email support. We provide a unique and distinct service for bereaved adults across the UK, run by the bereaved for the bereaved. Suicide recognises no social, ethnic or cultural boundaries, and neither do we. Our support and groups are open to all survivors of bereavement by suicide aged 18 years and over. Open hours: Monday to Friday, 9am to 7pm, and the contact number is 0300 111 5065

description: Restore Hope is a charity that supports local families. Join our Garden Group, an outdoor wellbeing group. organisation: Restore Hope Restore Hope Latimer is a family focused charity based at Latimer Park. A special space in the countryside set in the heart of the Chilterns, just outside Amersham and Chesham and has been operating since 2002 and has a proven record of bringing change and help to people in need. We believe in the value of healthy, happy and stable families. We also believe that no matter how bad a situation may seem there is always hope. Our vision is therefore that every struggling family in the Chilterns finds help and hope for the future. This is clearly a big aim and one that requires us to continually increase our influence, effectiveness and reputation. We aim to achieve our vision by advancing and developing the programmes that we offer and continually looking for ways to engage with those most in need. We operate a clear strategy, with deliberate focus and dogged determination. We empower and equip key volunteers to lead various elements of our work, and support a motivated core staff team. name: Rewind Therapy
description: Rewind Therapy is a didactic form of Clinical Hypnotherapy that can help alleviate the emotional effects of traumatic events. Rewind Therapy, known as "closure with disclosure", stands out from other therapies because you don't need to share the details of your experience. Rewind Therapy sessions are free for veterans, with concessionary sessions on Wednesday mornings. Contact me or visit my website for details.
organisation: Steph McGee Hypnotherapy Solution Focused Hypnotherapy uses a variety of modern techniques to help you bring about significant, positive change in your life. We focus on what you want to achieve and get you there in a relatively short period of time. Clients describe this as an enjoyable process in which we avoid going over painful past memories focusing instead on what is working well and future positive changes. It's not easy being a parent. And it’s painful for parents to see their child struggling but childhood anxieties such as fears and phobias are increasingly common. I always suggest an initial session with just the parent/guardian, which may in itself suffice. We can then move on to sessions with both you and your child if you need more help. I require that you are present throughout your child’s hypnotherapy. Hypnotherapy for children is a different process to adults, so I talk you through it beforehand. As a parent, you play a valuable role in helping your child. And you’ll be pleased to hear that children respond incredibly well to positive change and generally require fewer sessions than adults. When younger children are struggling it is sometimes more beneficial to work with you, the parent and support you in facilitating change that will help you facilitate the positive changes in your child. You are very welcome to phone me for a chat to decide what might be your best route. I offer a private service just outside of Oxford City. I do not book clients back to back and offer plentiful free parking for your convenience. Clients under the age of 16 must be accompanied by a parent or guardian. Hypnotherapy helps with anything that is in some way affected by the mind. It’s most commonly known for helping with anxieties, fear, phobias, low mood, confidence, bag habits, insomnia, eating disorders and disordered eating, pain and childbirth. Trauma (also know as PTSD or PTS) can be resolved with the Rewind Technique (RT). Trained by Dr MUSS, his RT method has a recovery rate of 89% after 1 session (veterans are helped for free). There is no need to discuss your trauma in any depth to use this technique. Steph McGee BSc, DSFH, HPD, Hyp Dip (Paediatrics) info@stephmcgeehypnotherapy.com https://www.stephmcgeehypnotherapy.com/

name: College Lake Nature Reserve | Tring
description: Once a chalk quarry, College Lake in Tring is now one of the Berks, Bucks, and Oxon Wildlife Trust's flagship nature reserves. An outstanding centre for wetland wildlife with a visitor centre, cafe, shop, bird hides, and trails. Voluntary contribution on entry.
organisation: Berks, Bucks and Oxon Wildlife Trust (BBOWT) One of the last remaining traditional floodplain meadows in England. This large Living Landscape covers an area between Oxford, Bicester and Aylesbury. It includes 48,400 hectares of woodland, mixed farmland and floodplain meadows across the boundary between Oxfordshire and Buckinghamshire. The entire area is ecologically linked through the River Ray, which rises in Quainton, close to Finmere Wood nature reserve, and flows west alongside some of the last remaining traditional floodplain meadows in England, to join the River Cherwell at Islip, north of Oxford. Since 1981 BBOWT (Berks, Bucks and Oxon Wildlife Trust) has been buying and restoring floodplain meadows in the upper reaches of the River Ray, and working with neighbouring farmers to create a stronghold for wading birds including curlew. info@bbowt.org.uk https://www.bbowt.org.uk/wildlife/living-landscapes/bernwood-forest-and-ray-valley-living-landscape

name: Colne Valley Regional Park
description: The Colne Valley Regional Park is the first substantial taste of the countryside to the west of London. The Park, founded in 1965, stretches from Rickmansworth in the north to Staines and the Thames in the south, and from Uxbridge and Heathrow in the east, to Slough and Chalfont St Peter in the west. A mosaic of farmland, woodland, and water with 200 km of rivers, canals, and over 60 lakes. Covering 43 square miles, the landscape is a mix of bustling towns, green spaces, and waterways, which are the first taste of the countryside immediately west of London. The Colne Valley Community Interest Company aims to highlight this fantastic and varied area, its history, rich landscape, and biodiversity. Many people live, work, and visit the Colne Valley, but too few realise it forms part of a vibrant regional park.

description: The Community Friendly Fridge at Oakridge Baptist Church is here to share local food and reduce waste. We welcome everyone, and no referrals are needed. Guests can share food and skills and connect with others; however, to minimise carbon emissions, we ask that visitors not travel long distances by car. Please note that food availability can be unpredictable; we cannot guarantee specific items, so we don’t want anyone to be disappointed. This is a self-referral system - please come in person and bring bags for 4-6 kg of provisions, depending on donations. The Community Friendly Fridge is open every Thursday from 10am to 12 noon, subject to supply. Donations are welcome, and self-referral enrolment is required. Together, let’s combat stigma by sharing food.

name: Community Impact Bucks
description: Community Impact Bucks is a local charity that helps people get involved and make a difference in Buckinghamshire communities. We help people find volunteering opportunities, charities, and not-for-profit groups to get started, be effective, and grow. We run Volunteer Bucks in partnership with Buckinghamshire Council. This allows people to browse and apply for volunteering roles and all news organisations to post and manage their volunteer roles directly. Since March 2020, this service has mobilised over 2000 volunteers wherever they are needed, from supporting the vaccination programme to delivering food to mentoring young people. You can register with the service to find out about current volunteering opportunities. Through our Voluntary, Community, and Social Enterprise Support Service, funded by Buckinghamshire Council, we help Bucks charities and voluntary groups with all aspects of running their organisations, offering tailored support, guidance, and training. You can request support if you know of a small charity or voluntary group that would benefit from this. We also directly support Buckinghamshire’s communities: our Pub Lunch Clubs, Gardening, and Handy Helpers services help people stay connected and live independently. Our special services for Village Halls, Community Buildings, and Community Transport Schemes help ensure people can access vital services.
organisation: Community Impact Bucks We support people and groups to get involved and make a difference in local Buckinghamshire communities. We do this by offering expert advice and training, helping people to find volunteering opportunities, and helping charities and not for profit groups to get started, be effective and grow. We also have a number of directly delivered community services that focus on supporting those most in need – the elderly, vulnerable, and socially isolated. As an independent charity, we are the Council for Voluntary Service, Volunteer Centre, and Rural Community Council for Buckinghamshire. We are also the parent company of Healthwatch Bucks, an independent local organisation set up by the government to ensure that decision-makers and health and social care services put the experiences of people at the heart of their work. Community Impact Bucks and Healthwatch Bucks are both here to help improve the lives of people who live in Buckinghamshire: Community Impact Bucks inspires, supports, and enables voluntary and community action in the county. Healthwatch Bucks improves health and social care services by listening to you. It makes sure that what you have to say is heard by the people who deliver services and it works with groups whose views are not always being heard. We work together to make Bucks a better place to live. info@communityimpactbucks.org.uk https://communityimpactbucks.org.uk/

name: Community Nurses for Children with a Learning Disability
description: We specifically work with children and young people who have a diagnosed learning disability. We are commissioned to see children and young people with a the Buckinghamshire GP as part of the Buckinghamshire, Oxfordshire and Berkshire West Integrated Care Board (BOB ICB). We are a small team of qualified nurses or those who have had extensive training and experience of working with people with Learning Disabilities. We work with families and agencies in various settings to improve health outcomes for children and young people with a learning disability. We are all experienced at working with families in the community. We aim to work with families, professionals, and other agencies to enhance the lives and well-being of children and young people who have learning disabilities. We help each child to meet their optimum physical, emotional and intellectual potential. We help families to work on difficulties they have with their child/young person’s behaviour, toileting, sleep, health promotion, or offer advice and support to families with a child who has been newly diagnosed with a learning disability. An Individual Care plan will be written by the allocated team member with strategies which will help the family to address these needs. We also: • consult with other professionals to help enhance a child/young person’s overall experience of services • give families information and advice, or signpost them to other resources and services when needed • support children/young people and their families through transition into adult services Our team works with children and young people in their own homes, schools and respite units (according to their needs). We have a collection of helpful resources: Children with a Learning Disability - Buckinghamshire: Parents Health for Kids website.

We are also invited to work with children and young people in groups in schools, to promote independence and healthy lifestyle choices. We have a service leaflet which we give out to all families who are referred to us, we have a number of leaflets that we also share with families that advise them about managing behaviour, sleep problems, toileting and signposting to other services. description: The Hub is our supported workshop providing unique opportunities for people with mild to moderate learning support needs. This is managed by an experienced coordinator responsible for planning activities tailored to each individual. The tasks are similar to those in the main workshop which may include: - Cleaning and refurbishing hand tools. - Sorting and packaging haberdashery, crafts, and wool. - General administrative work - Supporting our recycling efforts. Attendees learn valuable life lessons and skills, such as perseverance, patience, and teamwork by participating in meaningful tasks and seeing them through to completion. We also make sure to take time away from workshop duties to allow everyone to express themselves creatively through various arts and crafts projects. The Hub is a safe and secure environment for participants to get involved in and feel a sense of purpose and value for their contribution. It helps them make the steps towards employment or voluntary work and creates a supportive environment for them to develop friendships.

name: Community Paediatrics
description: Community Paediatricians are specialist children’s doctors with training and expertise in developmental paediatrics and disability, social paediatrics (child protection and children in local authority care), neurodevelopmental work (ADHD and ASD diagnostic assessments) and educational paediatrics (special educational needs). What they do: The Community Paediatricians assess and care for children with a wide range of needs and conditions, particularly children with developmental problems and complex needs. They have specific expertise in Neuro-disability, looked after children, child protection and school health and have specialist clinics for children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and autistic spectrum disorders. They work closely with colleagues in primary care, therapy services, CAMHS and local schools seeing children in outpatient clinics at both Wycombe and Amersham hospitals and Rayners Hedge in Aylesbury, as well as assessing children at home and school or nursery. Statutory role and Partnerships: Health partners also have a statutory duty to notify the Local Authority of any children who are under 5 years and who have special educational needs or a disability. This is so that the iSEND Team can review whether they are getting the appropriate support. In Buckinghamshire, this was formerly known as CHSU5 but is now called the Statutory Early Years Notification Process. Paediatricians complete a form with the parents, which is submitted via secure email to the Local Authority and allocated to one of three area iSEND Teams for discussion. Training and Qualifications: All of the Medical staff are fully registered with the General Medical Council (GMC). All of the Medical staff have the relevant training and qualifications in line with the GMC’s requirements. All nursing staff have qualifications and training in line with the requirements set out by the Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC). Getting a referral: The service accepts referrals from professionals involved with a child and a young person. For example, a referral may be made by a School or Nursery, Health Visitors, School Nurses, Therapists, GPs, Acute Paediatricians, Tertiary Centre or other Paediatricians from neighbouring hospitals.

name: Connection Support
description: At Connection Support our team of staff members and volunteers work alongside people to overcome life’s challenges. Why? Because our mission is to support everyone in our society to become safely and sustainably housed and live as independently as possible. And to do that we provide a wide range of services which offer support with homelessness, housing support, mental health, independent living, preventing isolation, parental mentoring, refugee resettlement, adult autism, and social prescribing. We recognise that every human being encounters challenges in life and we’re here to support anyone who finds themselves in a time of difficulty, either through directly offering our support, or helping them to find the right support elsewhere. We focus on you as an individual, to understand your circumstances, abilities and challenges so we can begin to support and equip you to build a better life. You tell us what you want to achieve, your goals and aspirations and we will work with you, providing practical and emotional support to help you to build the skills and confidence to deal with the ups and downs of life. By working collaboratively with other organisations, we provide tailored support and advice to a range of adults (young and old) and families in Oxfordshire, Buckinghamshire, and Milton Keynes, ensuring we achieve the best outcome for all our clients.

name: Connection Support
description: At Connection Support our team of staff members and volunteers work alongside people to overcome life’s challenges. Why? Because our mission is to support everyone in our society to become safely and sustainably housed and live as independently as possible. And to do that we provide a wide range of services which offer support with homelessness, housing support, mental health, independent living, preventing isolation, parental mentoring, refugee resettlement, adult autism, and social prescribing. We recognise that every human being encounters challenges in life and we’re here to support anyone who finds themselves in a time of difficulty, either through directly offering our support, or helping them to find the right support elsewhere. We focus on you as an individual, to understand your circumstances, abilities and challenges so we can begin to support and equip you to build a better life. You tell us what you want to achieve, your goals and aspirations and we will work with you, providing practical and emotional support to help you to build the skills and confidence to deal with the ups and downs of life. By working collaboratively with other organisations, we provide tailored support and advice to a range of adults (young and old) and families in Oxfordshire, Buckinghamshire, and Milton Keynes, ensuring we achieve the best outcome for all our clients.

name: Continuing Care Team for Buckinghamshire
description: The clinical commissioning group, which is responsible for arranging for health services locally, has responsibility for assessing children from birth to 18 years to determine if they need a package of continuing care. These children and young people may have very complex health needs. These may be the result of: congenital conditions long-term or life-limiting conditions disability serious illness or injury Children with such complex needs may need additional health support to that which is routinely available from GP practices, hospitals, or in the community. This additional package of care is called continuing care. Who is eligible? Any child or young person up to their eighteenth birthday who has a complex health need may be eligible. When a young person reaches 18, the NHS Continuing Healthcare arrangements apply. There are significant differences between children and young people’s continuing care and NHS Continuing Healthcare for adults. Although a child or young person may be in receipt of a package of continuing care, they may not be eligible for NHS Continuing Healthcare. The Clinical Commissioning Group (CCG) will assess any young person in receipt of continuing care when they are aged 16 to 17 years, to see if they are likely to be eligible for NHS Continuing Healthcare when they turn 18 (Transition). How can someone access continuing care? A referral can be made by any health professional or carer who feels a continuing care package may be required. When a child or young person is referred for an assessment, the CCG might first check if they are likely to need a full assessment. A health assessor will then collect evidence of the child’s needs, drawing on the advice of health and care professionals. A national framework provides guidance, and a set of categories of needs to support decisions on whether or not a child has a continuing care need. An important part of the assessment is to capture the preferences of the child or young person and their family. The assessment will look at the current care being provided but a decision on whether or not a child or young person has a continuing care need is based on the nature of their needs, rather that the care available, or whether or not they have a particular condition. Who decides? What happens next? The health assessor will make a case to a panel of experts, who decide based on the evidence, and the recommendation, if the child or young person has a continuing care need. A decision is usually made 6 to 8 weeks from referral. Depending on the decision, a package of care is then agreed; some of this care may be provided through existing services; some may need to be specially arranged. The CCG will keep the package of care under regular review to ensure the developing child or young person’s needs continue to be supported. A child or young person’s eligibility for continuing care may change as their needs change. After 18: When a young person reaches 18 years of age Continuing Care ends. An adult then may be entitled to NHS Continuing Healthcare. This is an ongoing package of health and social care that is arranged and funded solely by the NHS where an individual is found to have a primary health need. Such care is provided to an individual aged 18 or over to meet needs that have arisen as a result of disability, accident, or illness. Contact the NHS Continuing Healthcare Team.

local_offer: Continuing Care is a general term that describes a tailor-made package of care which is required over an extended period of time for children and young people with complex health needs which can arise due to congenital conditions, long term, life-limiting or life-threatening conditions, disability, or the after-effects of serious illness/injury. However, it is important to note that diagnosis of a particular disease or condition is not in itself a determinant of a need for continuing care. Continuing Care may be provided for children and young people whose health needs cannot be met by existing universal, targeted, or specialist health services. The aim of the care package is to support the child, young person’s parents or carers to manage their child/young person’s care at home and/or in other settings. It may require the provision of services from the NHS, social care, education, or other organisations to enable the person to function in the community. We are located in the center of the village of Haddenham. Our setting is in a large Bungalow. Ofsted Graded Good. About the Setting: We provide a professional childminding service in the comfort of our family home for all children aged 0 months plus giving your Little Hopper the opportunity to enjoy and achieve. We offer a very good educational structure through play including painting, play dough activities, dressing up, themed activities, wet and sand play, child's library accessible all the time, and general craft activities and cooking; meeting the needs of children of all age groups and abilities. Our mission is to provide a warm fun, friendly and relaxed environment where the children can thrive and feel part of the family. I'm a very caring, energetic and social mum and take the same enthusiastic approach in my childminding role. We take regular walks and attend many groups dependent on the weather such as Whizz Kidz indoor play center, Local Parks, Bucks Goat center, Haddenham Library, Wendover Woods, Tiggy Winkles, Tring Museum, Lynx Gym, Waddesdon Manor, Thomley Hall, Feeding the ducks and much more! We will work within our registration requirements and to EYFS (Early Years Foundation Stage 2021) at all times and to a very high and safe standard. We celebrate many different cultural festivals and are also able to provide a diet suitable for each child and young person. A little bit about Corinne (Main Practitioner): I live with my Partner, My son Ciarán born July 2011, Daughter Ehrin Born May 2021, Step Daughter Jessica Born July 2010 and Stepdaughter Florence Born December 2017. I love anything to do with Motorsport, Craft and Music. My Hobbies are playing the violin, singing and amateur photography. I have been a unit Leader for 18 years with Rainbows who are aged 5 to 7 and Brownies who are 7 to 11 years and Guides ages 10 to 14. I have babysat for friends and family for many years. I have experience working with disabled children and know basic sign language. I am happy to make reasonable adjustments to my home to accommodate a child with SEN.

local_offer: SEN and Disability; Local offer Here at Little Hoppers Daycare we specialise in the care of children and young people with additional needs alongside those who do not as part of our inclusive practice. Our Settings SENDCO is Corinne Banham who can be contactable on 07813 880 153 or via e-mail Corinne@littlehoppersdaycare.co.uk The Setting The setting is home based and is a large bungalow. The setting is registered for a maximum of 18 children under the age of eight. Of these 128 children a maximum of 9 maybe young children (A child is a young child until September following his 5th birthday) and there should be only 3 children under the age of one. Places are available for all ages however the setting is aimed at those not yet at school. Funded education (15 universal hours and 15 extended hours) for eligible 2, 3 and 4 year olds now being offered. Before, after school and holiday care is available for older children. The setting is open Monday to Thursday 7am to 7pm however times can be flexible to accommodate parent’s needs. Corinne and Trisha are registered childminders. Together they employ 2 part time assistant. All Staff members are supported by a PACEY Quality improvement Partner, based at the local Authority. They are the dedicated SENCO for the area. Corinne manages all aspects of the childcare setting and has set policies and procedures that are adhered to in order to meet OFSTED requirements. What the setting provides The setting is based in a private Bungalow and access is available at ground floor level through the front and back doors. The front door has a small step but the back door is level with the pavement All external and internal doors are wide enough to allow access for those with walking aids. For security, the front door is lockable with a key and also a safety chain and there is a Door bell that can be heard in the garden. The back door is also lockable with the key placed out of sight. Entrance to the garage from the garden is locked and so are the gates with the gate at the front locked with a combination padlock. There is room to park outside the building with on street parking or there is availability to park on the drive way. There is a family bathroom and children can use the potty as well as the toddler toilet seat. There is a separate walk in shower room that can be accessed by wheelchair. We have a changing unit for smaller children and all children who are too long or heavy for this are changed on a mat on the floor. The settings registration certificate and OFSTED poster are displayed in the setting. A policy booklet is available on request. The setting has a set of policies and procedures available for parents to look at. These are printed in English. For families that require it, an electronic or printed version can be provided using a font size of their choosing. We are also able to provide the book in audio if required. The local Children’s Centre along with the staff at PACEY are able to provide multilingual staff that can translate for parents speaking English as a second language. The setting is equipped with resources to cater for all areas of the Early Years Foundation Stage. Children have free choice of resources and are able to access them independently in our fully equipped playrooms. We have a secluded rear garden offering the children and young people time to enjoy the many toys and activities on offer and the fresh air. There is a large play frame with slide and area of grass along with hard standing for ride on toys. We have a water wall, Sand tray, Playhouse, Kitchen and mark making area available at all times with additional activities being set up daily. Access to the garden is free-flowing whatever the weather. Identification and early intervention What the setting provides Parents will be asked to complete a child record form detailing any additional needs, previous illnesses, dietary requirements or allergies their child may have. Parents are given and asked to sign a set of permission forms which include permission to administer medications, Outings and transporting children in the car. If an additional need is identified within these documents a Health care plan will be put into place. If any medication has to be administered on a long term basis we will undertake child-specific training for this. Children’s progress is closely monitored within the setting. Each child has their own learning journey which includes detailed written observations and links to the EYFS. This information is shared with parents on a regular basis and a progress check is completed some- time between the child’s second and third birthday. Where the progress check suggests that a child may be experiencing some difficulties or delay in their development this is shared with the parents and appropriate next steps are discussed. For some children, the next steps may involve targeting a specific area of development and planning additional opportunities for the child to have experiences designed to support the area of learning and development identified. This would then be reviewed to see if there had been any progression or whether additional steps need to be taken. For other children, the next step may also include developing a targeted learning plan where specific aims are developed with parents to support their child’s development. Referral to other agencies (with parents’ consent) for example, speech and language therapy service will also be considered at this time. Another next step would be to ask the Local SENDCO to visit the child at the setting and provide some additional advice and guidance to support in meeting the child’s needs. This visit would be supported by the Childminder, sure start Children’s Centre and Health visitor. Parental consent would also be sought first. The setting will then receive continued support via the SENDCO and Children’s Centre ensuring that all the child’s needs are met. Prior to a child starting school, a summative assessment is carried out and this information is given to the parents to share with the school. If parents have any concerns they have the opportunity to talk to the childminder at drop off and pick up times, or they can telephone, use text or email. Teaching and Learning – Practitioners and Practice What the setting provides The setting works within the framework of the EYFS. The setting is resourced according to the ages and needs of the children. The setting uses Development Matters and the Statutory Guidance for the EYFS along with characteristics of effective learning to plan provision and activities for the children in their care. The EYFS identifies three prime areas of learning and development and four specific areas of learning and development. In the 0 to 2 age bracket the prime areas of learning and development (Communication and Language, Physical and Personal, Social and Emotional Development) are the areas of focus. In the 2 to 3 age bracket, the prime areas remain significant but there is an emergence on the specific areas of development and learning. In the 3 to 4 age bracket, the prime areas continue to be a focus but there is an increasing balance between focusing on supporting children's development in these areas and the specific areas. Activities and provision are adapted to suit the needs of all children in each age bracket. For some children, a greater level of differentiation is required because they have additional educational needs. When children first start in the setting parents and any 3rd party practitioners are asked to highlight the development grid to create a baseline assessment. Continued observations and tracking using the EYFS are then regularly carried out so that a learning journey can be put together. Children and parents are able to access their learning journey at any time. A diary is also completed that outlines the child’s routine and activities. Parents can make comments in this diary and use it as a way of communicating. Children are actively encouraged to express their views. This is done by asking them open questions like, ‘what did you like about ………’. They are also encouraged to look back through their learning journeys or photos and share any feelings they may have. On their return after the weekend break, they are asked what they have done, where they have visited. and this is sometimes incorporated into future planning. Teaching and Learning - Provision and amp; Resources What the setting provides Each age group is provided with resources that are developmentally appropriate for their age and stage of development. The setting ensures that there are resources available that overlap with the age phase below and above so that children who are developing more slowly or more quickly can access resources appropriate to their stage of learning and development. The setting works closely with other professionals and they are encouraged to share their reports so that individual needs can be met. Where children need specialised equipment discussions would take place with parents and other agencies to see what could be provided. The setting regularly purchases new resources and these are bought with the needs of the children in mind. The setting accesses a number of playgroups in the local area. Risk assessments are completed for trips outside of the setting and all children’s individual needs and reasonable adjustments are made where necessary. All trips and outings are planned in advance and discussed with parents. Child developmental reviews What the setting provides: Parents are able to ask about their child’s development at any time. They have regular contact at drop off and pick up times and are also able to phone, text or email the setting. At the end of each term, parents are given a summary of their child’s development and a progress check is completed and shared with them sometime between their child’s second and third birthday. The setting carries out regular observations and links these to the EYFS. If a child is not developing as expected for their age then this would be highlighted in their learning journey and discussed with parents. Parents are actively encouraged to become involved in their child’s education and any comments are gladly received. Staff Training What the setting provides All staff are working towards their level 3 qualification in childcare and education. We are members of PACEY (professional association of childcare in early years) and attend regular training including safeguarding, food hygiene and paediatric first aid. description: Neurobears is a pre-recorded course for autistic young people and their safe adults. Made by autistic adults in collaboration with autistic young people. 12 easy-to-watch videos (a total of 90 minutes). Workbooks for children and workbooks for adults. So much positivity about what it means to be Autistic (whilst not glossing over the tough bits). The opportunity for your young person to truly get to know and understand themselves and use that to advocate for themselves. description: With state of the art equipment and enthusiastic staff on hand to help you, our gym is the perfect place to get fit. You can pay separately each time you go, or for a great deal you can sign up to our expressions fitness membership and gain exclusive benefits. Whether you are seeking to play competitively against others, for fun against friends, or just fancy a knock on your own our courts are here for you to take advantage of. organisation: Little Chalfont Community Library Little Chalfont Community Library is a local library operated and funded by people and businesses who live and work in the village. It works in the same way as a Buckinghamshire Council Library; you can use your existing library card or you can join at the library - membership is free. We have everything you would expect to find in a local library; information, recreation, education and culture. As well as a wide range of books, we offer a number of facilities, including: up-to-date adult fiction and non-fiction (including large print) a big selection of children's and teenage fiction audiobooks on both cassette and CD periodicals, newspapers and local information photocopying and laminating free public internet access computers and free wi-fi access We hold regular events such as children's sessions, film nights, books groups and computer classes. Community groups and local businesses can also hire the library. littlechalfontlibrary@gmail.com https://www.littlechalfontlibrary.org.uk/

local_offer: In compliance with the new SEN Code of Practice and SEND Reforms, there is a graduated approach to the identification, provision and support for all students deemed to require special educational provision to be made for them at Cressex Community School. All students identified as needing additional provision will be placed on the SEN Register under one single SEN category and progress monitored via Individual Provision Mapping (this replaces the categories of School Action and School Action Plus). This Policy will set out our commitment to raising the aspirations and expectations for all pupils with SEN, including those identified as Gifted or Talented and/or who would benefit from aspiration-raising programmes. The purpose of out policy document is to describe the provision we make for students identified as having a special educational need (SEN) and the principles by which we make that provision. For consistency and clarity the term SEN is used throughout this document. This school believes that every student has an entitlement to develop to their full potential. Educational experiences are provided which promote high achievement and personal development for each individual. The wide diversity of the school’s population is valued as a rich resource, which supports the learning of all. In this school, we recognise a student’s right to a broad, balanced, relevant and challenging curriculum, which is appropriate to their individual abilities, talents and personal qualities. https://www.cressex.org/186/documents-and-policies What outcomes does your setting, service or activity aim to achieve for children and young people with SEND and their families? description: Talkback has launched three new films on how people with learning disabilities and autistic people can stay safe in the online world. They have been designed to be used by families, schools, charities, and any organisation who would like support in explaining how to safe online. They are accompanied by easy-to-use training booklets. Autistic people and those with learning disabilities have as much right as anyone else to be online. However, alongside the many benefits to using the internet, there are also a number of risks. Because with access to technology comes the potential for cyberbullying, online grooming and risk of exposure to inappropriate content. Of course, this is a risk for all people using the internet, but the risk can be more profound for autistic people and those with a learning disability. As a result of increased vulnerability, tendencies towards obsessive compulsive behaviour and other social challenges. The resources are free. You can find out more about them by visiting the Talkback website via the link below.

name: The Accessible Workshop High Wycombe
description: The Accessible Workshop is a Talkback Social Enterprise Initiative that enables people with a learning disability or autism to build work skills and gain an understanding of how their skills and talents can be used to create positive social change. The Accessible Workshop covers a wide range of woodworking and practical skills. It also teaches people how to plan and manage projects, as well as how to market and sell. The income generated is then reinvested back into the group, or is used to aid charitable partners that we work with. Each individual works to clear and structured plans, with each project treated as a commissioned piece of work. From basic safety awareness around the home, through to repairing, creating, upcycling, and developing employment skills; The Accessible Workshop creates realistic progression pathways. Our Workshops in Aylesbury and High Wycombe cater for those of all abilities, taking into account a wide range of physical and learning needs. We use a wide range of commercial and DIY tools that enable people to repair, create, upcycle, and build skills for the world of work. We have a clear and safety focused competency framework in place around the operation of machinery and power tools. Development Stages: Awareness - Gain basic awareness of woodworking and DIY skills that can be used in everyday life. - Develop key Health and Safety awareness that will keep you safe. Core Skills - Develop the skills which will enable you to undertake a range of DIY tasks. - Be able to use a range of basic hand and power tools. Upcycle - Develop awareness of upcycling and how to turn junk into profit. - Learn skills relating to budgeting, marketing and selling a product. Create - Develop the skills to plan a project and construct items for home and garden use. - Use more advanced power tools and machinery. Employment - Develop essential employment skills. - Plan, construct and market products, while gaining the confidence and skills to work independently.

local_offer: At The Cressex Day Nursery, we aim to provide every child with a safe and stimulating environment where they are supported in reaching their full potential. However, on occasions, a child may require extra support from our dedicated SEN Support team. Our SEN Support team work closely with parents and other professionals to ensure consistent and appropriate levels of support are given to each individual child during their early years.  What outcomes does your setting, service or activity aim to achieve for children and young people with SEND and their families? Within the nursery we have two members of staff who are trained SENCOs. Both are very committed to the nursery and have many years of child care experience. Both SENCO's attend relevant training courses to keep them up to date and maintain their knowledge. With the consent of parents, we work alongside Speech and Language Therapists, Occupational Therapists, Physiotherapists, Educational Physiologists, Paediatricians and we also receive support from The Early Years Inclusion Team. All staff are encouraged to attend training courses to support and further their knowledge and the SENCO's attend termly SENCO Liaison Groups. What recent SEND-specific training has been completed by your staff and/or volunteers?  How do you involve parents and how can I get involved? We feel that it is important to create a positive partnership with all our parents and aim to work sensitively with parents, developing and understanding of their child's needs and developing a consistent approach to their care and development. As well as twice-yearly Parents Evenings, parents are invited in for regular review meetings where we can discuss their child's development in their next steps and any changes to their needs. How will you share information with me about my child’s progress? What is additional for children with SEND? We feel that it is very important for our staff to work alongside our parents to ensure we are providing consistent and effective care. Therefore, we aim to create strong parent partnerships and work together to support all children in our care. We hold regular meetings between parents, their child's key carer and the nursery SENCO, enabling us to review progress both at nursery and at home and to offer support for each other. These meetings can be arranged at any point throughout the year at the request of the parent or nursery staff and not just at pre-scheduled dates and Parent's Evenings. We encourage parents to take home their child's learning journey on a regular basis, so that they can see the progress being made and we value parental input into these documents. If appropriate, the child's key carer or nursery SENCO can attend appointments with other professionals or outside agencies along with parents to help ensure consistency and to offer support. We treat each child as an individual and we endeavour to ensure each child reaches their full potential at their own pace. We will not treat a child with disabilities less favourable and will make reasonable adjustments. Therefore activities and the nursery's physical environments can be adapted where necessary to support their needs. Staff will review progress on a regular basis and will document and feedback to the appropriate people to ensure consistency in the way progress is made. How accessible is the environment (indoors and outdoors)? The nursery is situated all on one level, with ramp access to the main door. All doorways and corridors are wide enough to accommodate wheelchairs and disabled toileting facilities are available for both children and adults. If necessary the layout of individual rooms can be altered to enable safe and easy access for all. Resources are clearly labelled and are easily accessible and personal belongings are stored allowing easy access to all. How can children and young people with SEND and their families start to use your service or activity? Before a child starts the Cressex Day Nursery, they are invited in for a series of settling in sessions to prepare them for joining us. If a child is coming to us from another setting, with parental permission, we would contact the setting and liaise with them to aid a smooth transition. Likewise, when the time comes for a child to move on from the nursery, we would liaise with the new setting, passing on relevant information and supporting the transition as best we can. Where necessary, we will carry out risk assessments and will devise action plans for new children joining the nursery and will make sure all relevant staff are aware of these. What future plans do you have for developing your SEND provision? Along with all our policies, we review our Admissions and Inclusion policies annually and make adjustments to them as we see necessary. Staff will continue to attend training courses to support their professional development and help them provide a high standard of childcare for all our children.

local_offer: We recognise that all learners benefit from quality first teaching and appropriate Ordinarily Available Provision (as outlined by Buckinghamshire Council). We set high expectations for all and believe that every student can achieve the desired learning outcome. To support learners to do this we ensure a well-planned curriculum, we are proactive, and we plan for and prepare appropriate adaptations in advance. We carefully consider the role of Assistant Teachers (ATs) within lessons, ensuring that students continue to develop independence in their learning. We also recognise the need to be reactive by responding and adapting our teaching in real time. By doing this, we can give all our students the best chance of achieving a deeper level of learning. Once a student has been identified as having a Special Educational Need or Disability, their individual needs will be shared with staff via a variety of means including Class Profiles, and Person-Centred Learning Plans. These documents will outline their needs and how they can be supported by teachers through Quality First Teaching. If a student requires targeted or specialised support or intervention outside of the usual curriculum, this will be identified in the SEND Support Plan and delivered through one or more of the interventions offered in school. The range of interventions we offer is varied and student-centred. Appropriate interventions are determined by the SEND team following analysis of each students' individual needs, which may be identified on their EHCP. We strive to provide the appropriate interventions for all students, whilst recognising that quality first teaching for students in the classroom with their peers is essential for good progress. The Orchards is a dedicated space at The Kingsbrook School designed to support the diverse needs of students in the mainstream school. It provides a quiet and structured environment for interventions based on individual student needs. The Orchards features regulation stations and a sensory room, providing students with the tools and spaces they need to manage their emotions and sensory needs effectively. These resources are essential for helping students maintain their well-being and readiness for learning throughout the school day. The Orchards is a hub for targeted interventions, where students can receive tailored support to address specific challenges and enhance their overall development. Our dedicated team works closely with each student to ensure they receive the personalised attention and resources they need to thrive both academically and emotionally. The Orchards also includes a social pod, offering a space where students can develop their social skills in a supportive environment at break and lunch time Within our school is The ARC, an Inclusion Unit that provides a specialist setting for students who need additional support with their Social, Emotional and Mental Health (SEMH). The ARC is a small, specialist setting, with places for 32 students in total across Y7-11, that operates as a "school within a school". Our vision, ethos and strong focus on character extends across this provision, where students access an adapted curriculum, targeted small-group teaching, therapeutic interventions and when appropriate, supported access to whole school lessons to support them to “achieve & flourish” from their unique starting points. Students with a school place in The ARC will have an EHCP identifying SEMH as a primary area of need and will have been placed in the Inclusion Unit (rather that the mainstream school) via the EHCP annual review and phase transfer process with Buckinghamshire Council. https://www.kingsbrook.org.uk/SEND/ What outcomes does your setting, service or activity aim to achieve for children and young people with SEND and their families?
